subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Visual Salience and Attention
description: One-minute skill: Visual Salience and Attention.

hook.text: A bright orange Buy Now button converts 32% more than a grey one. The product is the same.

buildup.text: Visual salience means making one element stand out. The brain's attention is drawn to contrast, color, and size.

discovery.text: Eye-tracking studies show users spend 80% of attention above the fold and gravitate toward the largest, brightest.

twist.text: Salience can also hide. Terms and conditions are grey, small, and at the bottom. Low salience is a design decision too.

climax.text: On any purchase page, look for what is hidden as carefully as what is highlighted.

punchline.text: What they make hard to see is what they hope you miss.

quiz.question: Why are terms of service displayed in small grey text?
options: To save space on the webpage
Low visual salience reduces the chance customers will read them
Legal requirements mandate that font size

details.summary: Visual salience determines what consumers notice first through contrast, color, size, and movement. Marketing designs use salience to direct attention toward desired elements like prices, buy buttons, and key product features while suppressing less favorable details.
details.whyItMatters: Attention is the gateway to all persuasion. No matter how compelling an offer is, it fails if consumers never notice it. Visual salience engineering is how marketers control the finite resource of consumer attention.
takeaways: High-contrast elements capture attention before content is consciously processed
Color, size, and isolation are the primary drivers of visual salience
Strategic salience directs consumer attention to desired decision factors

faq.question: How do marketers use visual salience to influence decisions?
faq.answer: By making favorable information large, colorful, and prominent while keeping unfavorable details small, gray, and peripheral. The buy button is bright; the terms and conditions link is tiny. Attention engineering shapes what consumers process first.

faq.question: Does visual salience work on experienced, aware consumers?
faq.answer: Yes. Salience operates at the pre-attentive level before conscious processing begins. Even consumers who know about attention manipulation still have their gaze drawn to high-contrast, large, or isolated elements first.
